detail.title: The Rightful Heirs of Sarah Schenirer

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bar Ilan University Faculty of Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Bar-Ilan University Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article examines the legacy of Sarah Schenirer, the pioneering founder of the Bais Yaakov girls' school movement in early 20th-century Poland. Schenirer, a seamstress from Kraków, recognized the widening gap between traditional Jewish education for boys and the lack of formal Jewish schooling for girls, which left young women vulnerable to assimilation and secularization. Despite initial opposition and ridicule, she established the first Bais Yaakov school in 1917, eventually gaining crucial rabbinic support from figures like the Hafetz Hayyim and the Gerrer Rebbe. The movement rapidly expanded across Europe, transforming women's Jewish education in Orthodox communities. Recounting Schenirer’s achievements raises a compelling question: Who are Schenirer's true spiritual heirs today? Are they the traditional Bais Yaakov schools that continue her institutional legacy, or those who have pushed further to open advanced Torah study—including Talmud and Hasidism—to women, as advocated by Rabbi Soloveitchik, the Lubavitcher Rebbe, and others?

title: A Danger to Self and Others: Consequences of Involuntary Hospitalization
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: A Danger to Self and Others: Consequences of Involuntary Hospitalization

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Every state in the country has a law permitting involuntary hospitalization if a person presents a danger to themselves or others as a result of mental illness. If a person reaches this high bar, the logic goes, they should be confined in a psychiatric hospital for treatment until they are stabilized. (The process is also sometimes called involuntary commitment, involuntary psychiatric hold, or sectioning.) Although there is no definitive national accounting, it is estimated that about 1.2 million involuntary psychiatric hospitalizations occur every year (Lee and Cohen 2021). This puts the magnitude on par with the 1.2 million individuals imprisoned in state, federal, and military prisons every year (Carson 2022). In a new Staff Report, we use data from Allegheny County, which includes Pittsburgh, to measure how psychiatric commitments are impacting an individual’s risk of danger to themselves or others, earnings, and housing.

title: A Spatially Structured Empirical Bayes Framework for Traffic Safety Countermeasure Evaluation
affiliations: McGill University, HEC Montreal, McGill University and Independent

detail.title: A Spatially Structured Empirical Bayes Framework for Traffic Safety Countermeasure Evaluation
detail.abstract: This study introduces a novel two-step, spatially structured Empirical Bayes (EB) framework for evaluating the safety effectiveness of traffic countermeasures, built upon the Network Process Convolution (NPC) model. The NPC employs a network-based Gaussian Process (GP) with reweighted kernel convolution to capture spatial correlation of collisions along road networks, enabling the assessment of both site-specific and network-wide treatment effects. In Step 1, spatial hyperparameters are estimated using only untreated sites and without covariates to ensure an unbiased prior structure. In Step 2, two NPC models sharing the fixed spatial hyperparameters are developed: one models observed post-treatment collisions at treated sites, and the other estimates counterfactual outcomes using untreated and pre-treatment data. Collision reduction is computed by comparing the two model outputs. A case study of Driver Feedback Signs (DFS) across 1,366 arterial and collector segments in Edmonton, using 10 years of collision data, demonstrates the framework’s utility. The proposed method estimates average reductions of 37.18% for total collisions, 35.75% for property-damage-only (PDO), and 37.09% for severe collisions, while also quantifying uncertainty at each site. This network-aware approach generalizes the traditional EB Poisson-Gamma (EB-PG) method by explicitly modeling spatial correlation, and establishes the foundation for more robust, network-sensitive safety analysis. Future research will focus on refining the methodology, extending validation to broader contexts, and improving generalizability to support data-driven transportation safety planning.

title: Fintech's Role in Democratizing Private Equity: Accessibility for Retail Investors
affiliations: Osmania University (OU)

detail.title: Fintech's Role in Democratizing Private Equity: Accessibility for Retail Investors
detail.abstract: Private equity (PE) has historically been reserved for institutional investors and ultra-high-net-worth individuals due to high capital requirements, illiquidity, and regulatory restrictions. With the advent of financial technology (fintech), new platforms are lowering entry barriers, enabling fractional ownership, and providing transparency. This paper investigates fintech's impact on democratizing private equity using empirical data, event studies, and regression analyses. Findings suggest fintech reduces minimum investments by 98%, increases retail participation nearly 3,900%, and generates an additional 0.85% IRR premium, albeit with a 12% higher drawdown probability. Policy implications emphasize SEC-mandated disclosures, AI-driven risk tools, and balanced regulation to ensure sustainable democratization.

title: Globalization and Gender Gap: The Role of Economic Globalization in Driving Gender Equality
affiliations: Istanbul University, UPF Barcelona School of Management, Necmettin Erbakan University/Faculty of Political Sciences/Department of Economics and Istanbul Medipol University

detail.title: Globalization and Gender Gap: The Role of Economic Globalization in Driving Gender Equality
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of economic globalization on gender inequality, using panel data from 106 countries between 2006 and 2022 and applying multiple econometric methods. Findings consistently show that deeper global integration is linked to narrower gender gaps. However, not all forms of globalization equally promote gender equality. Among the KOF sub-dimensions, Economic Globalization-especially its trade and financial components-emerges as the strongest and most consistent contributor to improvements in the Global Gender Gap Index (GGI). These effects are especially evident in developing countries, where trade and investment flows increase female labor market participation and help close wage gaps. A breakdown of GGI's four dimensions shows that globalization has the clearest impact on economic participation, while its influence on education, health, and political representation is limited or inconsistent. In these areas, domestic policies, cultural norms, and institutional structures often play a more significant role than international integration. Overall, the paper concludes that economic globalization can facilitate gender equality under certain conditions, but supportive national reforms and targeted initiatives remain essential to ensure progress across all domains of women's lives.

title: Time-to-Event Crash Severity Prediction at Highway-Rail Grade Crossings with Monotonic Neural Networks
affiliations: Widener University, North Dakota State University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Time-to-Event Crash Severity Prediction at Highway-Rail Grade Crossings with Monotonic Neural Networks
detail.abstract: Despite advances in highway-rail grade crossing (HRGC) safety, including the widespread adoption of active control devices, crashes at these intersections still result in severe outcomes. Conventional crash prediction models often fail to capture dependencies among severity levels, rely on assumption-driven and computationally intensive methods, and overlook the link between crash severity and time between events. This study introduces a predictive framework based on positive monotonic neural networks (MNNs) for modeling crash severity at HRGCs. The Neural Fine-Gray model is employed as a key implementation of the MNN framework to estimate the likelihood of crashes by severity level, eliminating the numerical integration required in conventional time-to-event approaches and thereby accelerating training and reducing computational burden. Unlike traditional machine and deep learning approaches that depend on resampling, the framework naturally handles imbalanced HRGC data by treating event-free records as right-censored. To examine the unexplored role of severity-level dependencies, four MNN-based architectures are developed to evaluate their impact on predictive accuracy and learning efficiency. Using a 29-year dataset of HRGC crashes in North Dakota, the results reveal trade-offs between prediction accuracy and computational demand. The cause-specific MNN achieves the highest accuracy for medium- and long-term horizons, making it suitable for safety design requiring minimal error, while the multi-head MNN excels in short-term predictions with the fastest convergence, making it ideal for web or machine-learning applications requiring low latency. The framework also enhances interpretability by uncovering paradoxical effects, such as the “adding flashing lights paradox” and the “adding stop signs paradox.”

title: The Association between Institutions and Innovation in Entrepreneurship: A Panel Data Study
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Association between Institutions and Innovation in Entrepreneurship: A Panel Data Study
detail.abstract: This paper empirically examines the relationship between institutions, specifically the rule of law, and entrepreneurship at two levels: general entrepreneurial activity and innovation-driven entrepreneurship activity. With hopes to add to the conversation about the effects of intuition in shaping the incentives around economic activity at the micro level, the aim of this paper is to shed light on how the strength of a country’s rule of law may inhibit or empower different types of entrepreneurial activity. A random effects model with country-level random intercepts was used to account for unobserved heterogeneity across an unbalanced panel dataset of 79 countries between 2012 and 2022. The results reveal a negative relationship between rule of law and general entrepreneurship, but a positive association with innovation-driven entrepreneurship. These results highlight an important policy trade-off: while strengthening rule of law institutions may reduce the overall volume of entrepreneurial activity, it appears to enhance the quality and innovative potential of the ventures that do emerge. Policymakers aiming to stimulate innovation should prioritize targeted institutional reforms rather than treating the rule of law as a uniform construct. Specifically, the results suggest that efforts to combat corruption and protect fundamental rights are positively associated with innovation-driven entrepreneurial activity, indicating that targeted institutional reforms in these areas may be particularly effective in fostering innovative entrepreneurship.

detail.abstract: This study contributes to growing calls for greater pluralism in economics by examining how gender shapes economists' normative and epistemological orientations. Drawing on original survey data from 2,425 economists across 19 countries, we document systematic gender differences in views on a broad range of issues. Female economists are significantly more likely to support progressive equity-oriented positions, challenge mainstream assumptions, and endorse pluralistic approaches to inquiry. We also find stark gender differences in political ideology: women are far more likely than men to identify as left-leaning-particularly far-left-while men disproportionately align with centrist or right-leaning ideologies. These ideological divides account for some of the gender differences in views, underscoring the mediating role of political ideology. However, the influence of ideology itself varies by gender: moving rightward on the ideological spectrum reduces support for some progressive positions more sharply among men than women. This suggests that gendered experiences inform distinct interpretive frameworks that persist even within shared ideological categories. Taken together, our findings highlight that gender diversity in economics is not merely demographic but epistemic—and that realizing its transformative potential requires institutional environments that value and legitimize dissenting and underrepresented perspectives.

title: The Role of Labour Law in Protecting Informal Sector Workers in Urban India

detail.title: The Role of Labour Law in Protecting Informal Sector Workers in Urban India

detail.abstract: India's urban economy relies on millions of informal workers, including domestic workers, construction labourers, street vendors, waste pickers, and an expanding cohort of gig/platform workers who provide essential services yet often lack formal contracts, social security, workplace safety, and a legal voice. This Article critically examines how existing law (particularly the new Labour Codes and sector-specific statutes) fails many urban informal workers, the enforcement hurdles that turn statutory rights into "Paper promises," and the human consequences for wages, safety, and collective bargaining. Drawing on national surveys, NGO reports, judicial observations and sectoral case studies, the Article concludes with concrete, implementable reforms to extend meaningful protection to India's urban informal workforce.

title: The Use and Design of Emissions Targets and Internal Carbon Pricing: Evidence from a Global Sample
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Economics, Finance, Accounting (EFA)

detail.title: The Use and Design of Emissions Targets and Internal Carbon Pricing: Evidence from a Global Sample
detail.abstract: Using broad-sample CDP data, we provide novel evidence on the sources of variation in firms' use and design of emissions targets and internal carbon pricing (ICP), two theoretically motivated internal mechanisms for firms to reduce their emissions. We find that a rich set of variables capturing climate-related risk exposures explains the highest proportion of variation in emissions target and ICP usage. Moreover, these risk exposures influence the use and design of targets and ICP in several intuitive ways. Our results also indicate that firms' emissions target and ICP choices are influenced by external pressure and the importance of other risks, as well as boardlevel climate preferences. Lastly, we find that emissions targets and ICP are complements, with ICP use most pronounced when firms' targets imply a strong commitment to reducing emissions. Our findings suggest that many (but not all) firms' emissions targets and ICP choices are intentional rather than symbolic.

reference: Columbia Science and Technology Law Review, Forthcoming
title: Pharmaceutical Mergers: Do We Have the Right Cure?
affiliations: UC Law, San Francisco, UC Law, San Francisco, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and UC Law, San Francisco

detail.title: Pharmaceutical Mergers: Do We Have the Right Cure?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Science and Technology Law Review, Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
Few federal agencies wield tools more powerful than the Federal Trade Commission’s authority to review—and deny—proposed mergers between companies. This authority is powerful for a reason: Large mergers can be uniquely harmful to the United States economy, potentially reducing competition, undercutting consumer choice, and inflating prices. 

The pharmaceutical industry is particularly sensitive to merger harms, given the limited number of competitors and the inelasticity of demand for prescription drugs. As a result, when pharmaceutical companies seek to merge, the FTC often requires that one of the companies divest ownership of certain drugs not yet on the market—so-called “pipeline” drugs––to a third party.

FTC evaluations deem the pipeline divestiture program a complete success. But does it really work? As a client once said when asked this question, “It depends on what you mean by ‘it’ and ‘work.’” In prior research, the FTC determined the success of a divestiture based solely on whether it occurred––rather than whether it meaningfully preserved competition post-merger. Our first-of-its-kind study reveals that pipeline divestitures have not in fact worked. Using conservative measures, our analysis shows that 81% of divested pipeline products fail to attain even a 1% share of their relevant markets. 

But all is not lost: With a few key changes, drug divestiture can indeed achieve its intended effects. We recommend that the FTC require either a “crown jewel divestiture” (selling the on-market product, not the pipeline product) or a “skin in the game divestiture” (if the pipeline product fails, the company divests its on-market product).

title: Key Policy Changes Affecting Executive Compensation Contracts

detail.title: Key Policy Changes Affecting Executive Compensation Contracts
detail.abstract: The piece presented here is a small part of a much extended and detailed project that I have been working on at the Stigler Center with Prof. Raghuram Rajan and Prof. Luigi Zingales. Herein, I present a comprehensive overview of the key regulatory and tax policy changes that have affected executive pay contracts starting from 1950 till 2020. The piece is divided into three sections. Section 1 – This section deals with all the key tax policy and regulatory changes that have taken place from 1950 onwards, which have affected executive pay contracts in a serial manner. The section covers all the key policy changes in detail. Section 2 – This sectioncovers the impact of the policy changes discussed in Section 1 and goes into deeper detail in terms of explaining how and why the policy changes have affected executive pay contracts andhow firms have responded and adapted themselves to these changes. The section covers the time 1970 to 2002 as it is the most interesting period in terms of understanding executive pay contracts and executive pay levels. As it is during this period, we observe moderate to exponential growth in CEOs’ average and median pay levels as it has been presented extensively in the executive compensation literature. In Section 3 – we study the period 2002 to 2006 when everything unraveled, from the Enron Scandal to the options backdating scandal. This section explores how the government tackled one of US Corporate history’s biggest corporate frauds and scandal. Overall, herein, I present these events along with data and changes in corporate governance to illustrate how important it is to consider political factors when studying executive compensation and trying to explain the trends over the years. This piece is part of a much more elaborate project that I have been working on, which revolves around understanding how the purpose of the modern-day corporation has evolved over time and what factors have led to this evolution. Tax policy and regulatory changes are just one dimension of this project but are one of the key dimensions that has allowed us to understand how politics and democratic institutions work in tandem with corporations, resulting in sometimes good results and, more often than not, bad results.

title: Russian Regional Unemployment: How Resilient is the Beveridge Curve to the Ukrainian War and Pandemic?

detail.title: Russian Regional Unemployment: How Resilient is the Beveridge Curve to the Ukrainian War and Pandemic?
detail.abstract: Russian regional unemployment is explained by a Beveridge curve before the pandemic and through the wartime years up to 2024. The exceptionally low regional unemployment rates of the wartime economy may be fundamentally changing the Beveridge curve in 2023 with how far a region is from Moscow no longer as important as it was historically. Pre-pandemic economic development of a region lowers the unemployment rate throughout 2018–2023. Historically high human capital of a region loses significance 2022–2023 as the labor market becomes very tight. No evidence was found that military recruitment bonuses are associated with a region’s unemployment rate though some extremely poor regions appear to have much higher bonuses.

title: The Polluter Pays Principle in India: A Critical Analysis
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Polluter Pays Principle in India: A Critical Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the challenges and inconsistencies in applying the Polluter Pays Principle (PPP) in India. First introduced in 1972 by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the PPP is based on the idea of cost internalization, wherein the polluter bears the expenses of environmental restoration and compensation, rather than the government or general public. India with its less stringent environmental regulations have made it a potential "pollution haven". Therefore, a more effective implementation of the PPP is crucial to avoid environmental degradation. The paper identifies two major inconsistencies in the judicial application of the principle. First, the courts' approach often lacks a coherent framework, as they tend to apply PPP based on the "inherent polluting nature" of activities rather than the specific legal definition of pollution. Second, the methodology for calculating compensation is ambiguous and inconsistent. Courts often resort to "limited guesswork" to determine fines, often resulting in negligible penalties that fail to internalize external costs. This approach bases compensation on the polluter's ability to pay rather than the actual extent of environmental harm, which undermines the principle's core objective of restitution. To address these issues, the paper proposes a more scientific and standardized approach such as risk assessment and expert committees modelled after the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, to compute compensation based on actual environmental and health impacts. These measures would help align the PPP with the principle of restitution and achieve its ultimate goal of promoting a more sustainable way of life.

title: Resilience in Flux: Rethinking Small-State Strategy through Charles Lobell's Small States in a Shifting International Order

detail.abstract: The review article on Charles Lobell's book "Small States in a Shifting International Order" explores how small states navigate complex global dynamics by focusing on the interplay of security, legitimacy, and influence. It highlights Lobell's innovative approach, which combines comparative case studies from various regions, including Europe and the Middle East, to identify strategic behaviors that small states employ to maintain their agency despite structural challenges. The article emphasizes the importance of governance, international partnerships, and economic diversification as key factors for small states to enhance their resilience and influence. It also critiques the book for underestimating domestic political dynamics and historical contexts that shape small-state strategies, suggesting that a more integrated approach could provide a deeper understanding of their roles in international relations. Overall, the review underscores the need for small states to adapt and innovate in response to ongoing global changes while balancing their internal governance challenges.

title: The Role of African Cabinet Ministers: Missteps and Mismanagement
affiliations: Durban University of Technology and Durban University of Technology

detail.title: The Role of African Cabinet Ministers: Missteps and Mismanagement
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the role of African cabinet ministers, focusing on the missteps and mismanagement that often characterize their tenure. As key government figures, ministers are responsible for implementing policies and managing public resources. However, many faces significant challenges that hinder their effectiveness, contributing to broader governance issues across the continent. The research outlines the constitutional and operational responsibilities of cabinet ministers in various African nations, highlighting failures due to inadequate training, lack of resources, and political interference. Through secondary studies and case analyses from 44 scholarly articles from 2010 - 2025, the paper illustrates how mismanagement and corruption undermine public trust and hinder developmental progress. The study examines systemic factors contributing to these missteps, including political patronage, weak institutional frameworks, and insufficient accountability mechanisms. It emphasizes that many ministers operate in environments where short-term political considerations overshadow long-term developmental goals, often prioritizing personal or party interests over public welfare. Additionally, the paper discusses the impact of ineffective leadership on critical sectors such as health, education, and infrastructure. By analyzing specific policy failures and their repercussions, the study reveals the urgent need for reform in ministerial roles and accountability structures. In conclusion, the paper argues that addressing the mismanagement of cabinet ministers is essential for improving governance and fostering sustainable development in Africa. By advocating for enhanced training, stronger institutional support, and greater accountability, the findings aim to inform policymakers and stakeholders committed to strengthening governance effectiveness. Ultimately, the paper seeks to contribute to the discourse on enhancing the role of cabinet ministers as agents of positive change in African societies.

detail.abstract: We document novel stylized facts regarding updating of households' inflation expectations. Using two randomized controlled trials fielded in the US and Germany where signals in the form of professionals' inflation forecasts have different perceived levels of precision, we show that households react more to information with higher levels of precision, in line with Bayesian updating. However, in contrast to Bayesian updating, they mostly respond differently to these signals in the decision to update expectations (extensive margin) and not in the size of the adjustment (intensive margin). The extensive margin also displays a pronounced asymmetry: Households more frequently update their expectations when the signal is above the prior compared to when the signal is below the prior. We propose a model where households' inflation expectations exhibit state-dependent inattentiveness to inflation signals. In times of high uncertainty, elevated inflation expectations may persist due to the increased information processing costs of uncertain inflation signals and the relatively smaller welfare losses of not adjusting expectations when signals are below priors (disinflations) compared to when signals are above priors (accelerating inflation). Our model provides microfoundations for the asymmetric loss function that is commonly assumed to explain biases in inflation expectations.

title: The Organizational Law of Life: How Cellular Systems Reveal Organizational Inevitabilities

detail.title: The Organizational Law of Life: How Cellular Systems Reveal Organizational Inevitabilities
detail.abstract: Biological science has long focused on genes, molecules, and biochemical pathways, while organization theory has examined firms, institutions, and societies. Yet both confront the same fundamental question: how do collectives endure? This article advances the claim that the Black Belt OS (BB-OS)-a proposed universal structural law of human organization-operates not only in social systems but also at the cellular level. We demonstrate that every living cell instantiates the nine essential processes, forty-five irreducible steps, and ninety-eight specific actions that constitute the OS. Each process is illustrated with its cellular counterpart: implementation through gene expression and differentiation, people through the recruitment and integration of organelles and proteins, attraction through receptor-mediated signaling, conversion through biochemical cascades, admission through selective membrane transport, execution through protein synthesis and replication, results through feedback and checkpoints, finance through energy metabolism, and relationships through intercellular communication and symbiosis. We argue that these manifestations are universal, irreducible, interdependent, and falsifiable. The absence of any action leads to cellular collapse, while no action duplicates another. By mapping the full 9-45-98 structure onto cellular life, we provide evidence that the OS is not an invention of human management but a supracontextual law of collective order. The implications are profound: organization is revealed as a grammar of life itself, spanning from cells to corporations.

title: Valuing Questions When Answers Are Cheap: A Dynamic Framework for the Economics of Curiosity in the AI Era
affiliations: Independent Research

detail.title: Valuing Questions When Answers Are Cheap: A Dynamic Framework for the Economics of Curiosity in the AI Era
detail.abstract: In an era increasingly defined by Artificial Intelligence (AI), the marginal cost of obtaining answers is rapidly approaching zero. This paradigm shift creates an economic paradox: as answers become abundant, the ability to formulate meaningful questions-a manifestation of curiosity-emerges as a critical and scarce resource. However, classical and neoclassical economic frameworks lack the tools to formally define, measure, and value curiosity as a productive asset. This paper seeks to fill this theoretical gap by proposing a foundational framework for "Curiosity Economics." We introduce the concept of "Curiosity Capital" as a distinct form of human capital. We then develop and compare two quantitative models for its measurement: a static model based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence, and a novel dynamic model. We present this dynamic model in both its ideal continuous integral form and its practical discrete summation form. Through a detailed case study, we demonstrate the model's application and reveal a "path independence" property, which we argue exposes the core components of curiosity. This analysis leads to the proposal of a second-order model for future research. The paper concludes by discussing the profound implications of this framework for education policy, corporate innovation strategy, and the valuation of long-term scientific research.

title: The Celtic Theory of the Origins of Rus' as an Alternative to Normanism and the Concept of the «Old Rus' Ethnicity»
affiliations: Mukachevo State Agrarian College

detail.title: The Celtic Theory of the Origins of Rus' as an Alternative to Normanism and the Concept of the «Old Rus' Ethnicity»
detail.abstract: The aim of this study is to provide a critical analysis of the Normanist theory of the origin of Rus' and the concept of «Old Rus' ethnicity» («davniorus'ka narodnist'») within the context of the Celtic theory. The author questions the prevailing paradigms that link the emergence of Rus' exclusively to Scandinavian influence or to a unified Slavic ethnic foundation. Particular attention is devoted to the hypothesis that the ethnonym «Rus'» derived from the Finnish word «Ruotsi», used to describe Swedish merchants. This assumption is critically re-evaluated based on historical and linguistic evidence. The novelty of the study lies in its systematic revision of conventional interpretations of the origin of Rus' through the integration of the underexplored Celtic factor-specifically the role of the Celtic Ruthenians. The paper analyses historical evidence and toponymic parallels in Europe and the Dnipro region in general, along with archaeological data from the Przeworsk and Chernyakhiv cultures, which attest to Celtic migration and integration in Eastern Europe between 469 and 562 CE or earlier. A new interpretation of medieval sources and place names is proposed, enabling a rethinking of early Rus' formation within a broader European context. Conclusions. The concept of «Old Rus' ethnicity» («davniorus'ka narodnist'») is shown to be an ideological construct that does not withstand scholarly scrutiny. The traditional claim of a homogeneous East Slavic community in the 10th-12th centuries is based on artificial generalisations and disregards the linguistic, cultural, and ethnic diversity of Rus'. Unlike the Normanist theory-developed within the framework of imperial historiography and relying largely on late and questionable sources-the Celtic theory presents a more robust and verifiable source base, encompassing linguistic evidence, Celtic toponymy, and material indicators of cultural interaction. The study argues that the formation of Rus' was the result of a complex ethno-cultural synthesis in which the Celtic element played a structurally significant-not peripheral-role.

title: The Architecture of Failure: How International Diplomacy Perpetuates the Palestine-Israel Conflict
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title: The Architecture of Failure: How International Diplomacy Perpetuates the Palestine-Israel Conflict
detail.abstract: This manuscript examines the Palestine-Israel conflict through a provocative lens: as a deliberate "con game" orchestrated by successive great powers over the past century. The research reveals a consistent pattern wherein the British Empire, United Nations, United States, and now a broader Western coalition have each made contradictory promises to multiple parties while maintaining strategic ambiguity that serves their own interests rather than conflict resolution. The analysis proceeds chronologically through two major phases. First, it examines the foundational period (1917-1973), revealing how British triple-dealing through the Balfour Declaration, McMahon-Hussein correspondence, and Sykes-Picot Agreement. Second, it analyzes the "peace process" era (1993-present), demonstrating how the Oslo Accords. The study's key finding is that the Palestine-Israel conflict has become too useful to too many external actors to actually resolve. Arms manufacturers, regional autocrats seeking legitimacy, great powers maintaining influence, and international organizations sustaining themselves on crisis management all benefit from perpetual instability. The recent recognitions of Palestinian statehood by Western nations represent not progress but the latest iteration of diplomatic theater that changes nothing on the ground. The conclusion is sobering everyone knows what a just solution looks like-two states based on 1967 borders, shared Jerusalem, and negotiated refugee compensation-but this known solution remains unimplemented because permanent crisis serves more interests than permanent peace. Until this perverse incentive structure changes, the "con game" will continue, with Palestinians and Israelis remaining pawns in a game whose rules were written by others for purposes that have nothing to do with their wellbeing or security.

title: Investment Governance Standards (IGS): Measuring Discipline via the Discipline Disclosure Index (DDI) and Governance Adherence Ratio (GAR Ratio™)
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Investment Governance Standards (IGS): Measuring Discipline via the Discipline Disclosure Index (DDI) and Governance Adherence Ratio (GAR Ratio™)
detail.abstract: Traditional fund evaluation focuses on outcomes—returns, Sharpe ratios, factor exposures—while governance discipline has remained largely qualitative. This paper introduces two complementary governance metrics: the Discipline Disclosure Index (DDI), derived from public disclosures, and the Governance Adherence Ratio (GAR Ratio™), an audit-grade certification of adherence to stated mandates and risk controls. Using a pilot sample of mutual funds, we show that governance discipline is largely orthogonal to efficiency measures (near-zero correlation with Sharpe ratios) and provides modest downside protection during stress periods (high-discipline quartiles lost ~2.5 percentage points less in 2022). Pilot regressions confirm no redundancy between Sharpe and governance scores, supporting discipline as a distinct dimension of evaluation. Together, DDI and GAR form the foundation for Investment Governance Standards (IGS), analogous to the roles Sharpe ratios and GIPS play in performance reporting. We invite replication and extension across broader datasets, market cycles, and asset classes to formalize governance discipline as a measurable standard in asset management.

title: The Poverty of Attention: Mapping Inequality in the Age of Digital Abundance

detail.title: The Poverty of Attention: Mapping Inequality in the Age of Digital Abundance
detail.abstract: This report investigates the emerging phenomenon of "attention poverty" in the digital age, examining how the abundance of information and digital platforms contributes to an unequal distribution and allocation of human attention. Drawing upon Herbert Simon's foundational concept of attention as a scarce resource and Daniel Kahneman's theories of cognitive load, this study maps the disparities in attention management across different demographic groups, particularly Generation Z and adults . Through a hypothetical survey and simulated data analysis, we illustrate how digital Yeah, really enjoyed it too Aslan! Was super fun talking about economics, academics, culture and future stuff, characterized by constant stimulation and algorithmic curation, lead to fragmented focus, impulsivity, and decision fatigue, thereby creating a new form of inequality distinct from traditional wealth disparities. The report highlights the societal implications of this attention imbalance, including its impact on productivity, mental well-being, and informed decision-making. We propose policy and practical implications, advocating for enhanced attention literacy, workplace reforms, and ethical design principles for digital platforms to foster a more equitable and sustainable attention economy.

title: Fast-spiking neurons in monkey orbitofrontal cortex underlie economic value computation
affiliations: University of Tsukuba, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Tsukuba - Medical Sciences and University of Tsukuba - Division of Biomedical Science

detail.title: Fast-spiking neurons in monkey orbitofrontal cortex underlie economic value computation
detail.abstract: Inhibitory interneurons are fundamental constituents of cortical circuits that process information to shape economic behaviors. However, the role of inhibitory interneurons in this process remains elusive in the core cortical reward region, the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Here, we show that presumed parvalbumin-containing GABAergic interneurons (fast-spiking neurons, FSNs) resemble regular-spiking pyramidal neurons (RSNs) in computing economic value. While monkeys perceived a visual lottery for probability and magnitude of rewards, identified FSNs comprised 12% of OFC neurons, showing high-frequency firing rates and wide dynamic ranges, both are key intrinsic cellular characteristics regulating cortical computation. We found that FSNs showed similar neural signals to RSNs in encoding probability and magnitude information. Unambiguously, both neural populations signaled the expected values, but RSNs processed the reward information more strongly, governed by the dynamic range. Thus, shared information processing between FSNs and RSNs may provide a common cortical framework for computing economic value.

detail.abstract:
Narratives in American history, politics, and economics-even those by the most accomplished researchers-often resemble donuts: at their core lies a hole that no amount of sweet speculation can truly fill. They say almost nothing about the financing behind even the most pivotal American political campaigns and elections. Both history and the social sciences suffer greatly when facts are missing and wild guesses take their place. INET's new data archive of historical political finance records at the National Archives marks a major step toward filling this factual void. It assembles all campaign finance reports filed by political parties and presidential candidates up to 1974, the year before the Federal Election Commission was established. A few additional files, including one from the FEC for 1976, are also included, as detailed below.

This INET Working Paper outlines what users need to know to navigate the archive effectively and locate the data they require. The files themselves can be found here.

title: The Dirty Game of Growth: Shadows Behind the Shiny Numbers
affiliations: International Institute of Islamic Economics (IIIE), International Islamic University Islamabad

detail.title: The Dirty Game of Growth: Shadows Behind the Shiny Numbers
detail.abstract:
Growth has become the global currency of achievement. Governments mark the rising GDP growth rates each year as if they were scorecards of national triumph, while global institutions position nations on the basis of their growing economies. But beneath the brassy numbers lies a hidden reality—a dirty game of growth. This is not just a game of the intrinsic boom and bust of markets; it is expertly constructed, prolonged, and magnified by a coalition of actors: business elites who gain from unregulated growth, corporations that offload costs, and policymakers who spin illusions to calm public perception. At the core of it is financialization, loopholes in industrial policy, and utilitarian deployment of media to divert the masses with selective tales of triumph. What comes out of it is a warped image of progress, one that conceals its real cost.

From China's ghost cities to India's demonetisation, from Brazil's soy-fueled deforestation to Bangladesh's fast-fashion explosion, and from America's housing bubble to its glorious burst, the instances are aplenty. These examples show a general contradiction: although the benefits of greater riches are enjoyed by a privileged elite, the poor, the labourers, and the environment pay the maximum penalty. The dirty game succeeds because it offers immediate growth, but the secret price is revealed subsequently in the form of crises, displacement, and irreversible destruction.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the efficacy of FinTech-based programs in enhancing financial inclusion for SMEs in Kenya, a global epicenter of digital finance innovation. Through a qualitative analysis of leading platforms-categorized as digital-first lenders, MNO-led services, and governmentbacked initiatives-we identify a fundamental FinTech Inclusion Paradox: the very features that enable unprecedented access (speed, convenience, and algorithmic credit scoring) can simultaneously heighten the risk of over-indebtedness. Our findings reveal that financial literacy components remain largely supplementary or implicit, failing to mitigate these risks effectively. This is partly explained by platform business models where revenue is linked to transaction volume, creating a misalignment of incentives with long-term user financial health. The paper concludes that a paradigm shift from measuring success by loan volume to SME financial health is necessary. We propose a regulatory and design framework that mandates the integration of proactive, behavioral science-informed educational features to align platform incentives with sustainable user outcomes.

title: Reflexivity in Financial Markets: A Theoretical Framework Extending the Black-Scholes Model

detail.title: Reflexivity in Financial Markets: A Theoretical Framework Extending the Black-Scholes Model
detail.abstract: Extensive research has been conducted on the creation of models to predict market movement, with the Black-Scholes model being a cornerstone. The Black-Scholes model has been an integral part of modern financial theory, providing a mathematical framework for option prices under the assumption of exogenous market dynamics. However, in practice, financial markets are reflexive: Trading strategies based on mathematical models take as input the very variables that were affected by investing using these models. This challenges the core assumption of market efficiency in traditional financial theory. This research proposes a framework to formally introduce reflexivity into the Black-Scholes model. Specifically, we explore three mechanisms through which reflexivity alters market dynamics: (i) predictability of Brownian motion when trader dependence on mathematical model introduces path dependence, (ii) deviation of the drift coefficient from risk-free rate in a risk-neutral world due to large-scale institutional model use, and (iii) endogeneity of volatility. By reformulating the stochastic differential equation for asset price to include the above reflexivity-induced changes, we can show how reflexivity fundamentally alters option pricing dynamics. This framework advances the literature on market reflexivity, originally popularized by George Soros, by providing a formal mathematical structure linked to option pricing theory. The paper offers a pathway to rethink volatility estimation, systemic risk amplification, and the limits of using mathematical models in the financial market under the assumption that inputs are exogenous. This paper highlights the need for paradigm shift: the market cannot be assumed exogenous when the widespread use of mathematical models for investments actively shapes the inputs that are fed into the same models.

detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Greek businesses-for-sale market, based on all 517 active listings collected from Χρυσή Ευκαιρία (pronounced “Chrysi Efkairia”), a leading online platform for business transfers in Greece, as of September 2025. We examine market structure across sectors, geographic regions, business age, and exit motivations, and analyze pricing dynamics to identify patterns of value concentration and liquidity. Findings indicate significant sectoral concentration, with cafés, hair salons, and restaurants comprising the majority of listings, and pronounced geographic clustering in Athens and select urban hubs. Pricing exhibits high skewness, with capital-intensive sectors commanding substantially higher valuations, while smaller service-oriented businesses display moderate, consistent pricing. Investor-focused insights reveal that mature businesses offered for retirement present potential acquisition opportunities with defined risk-return profiles. The analysis contextualizes results within the Greek economic, social, and regulatory environment, providing both descriptive and practical frameworks for valuation, market assessment, and strategic investment decision-making.

title: Additionality in Agri-Environmental Programs: Panel versus Cross-Section Estimates

detail.abstract: Agri-environmental programs aimed at working farmland have played an increasingly significant role in agricultural support policies within developed countries. A critical issue that correspondingly arises is the efficiency of these programs in allocating spending, particularly regarding the additionality of agri-environmental subsidies. This paper focuses on the Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) in Maryland, specifically examining subsidies for the installation of riparian buffers. We provide estimates of additionality using two methods: (i) a first-difference estimator applied to panel data and (ii) a shift-share instrumental variable (SSIV) estimator in cross-sectional data. Our results suggest that CREP offers modest additionality, with estimates ranging from 65% to 70%. These estimates prove robust across a variety of model specifications. The empirical strategy employed, particularly the SSIV estimator, holds potential for broader applications across various voluntary program evaluations.

title: Liquidity and Spatial Spillovers of Accessory Dwelling Units in Housing Markets
affiliations: University of Connecticut, University of Connecticut, University of Connecticut - Department of Finance and California Lutheran University, School of Management

detail.title: Liquidity and Spatial Spillovers of Accessory Dwelling Units in Housing Markets
detail.abstract: Housing market liquidity, measured by the length of time a home remains on the market (TOM), reflects a property's overall desirability. This study investigates how the presence of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) affects housing liquidity. We hypothesize that ADUs function as an "inferior good"-an attribute that becomes less desirable as potential buyers' incomes rise, due to shifting priorities from income generation toward amenity preservation. We also hypothesize that properties in lower-income neighborhoods experience increased liquidity when ADUs are nearby. Using sales data from the City of Los Angeles (2017-2021), we find that the effect of ADUs on TOM varies significantly by neighborhood income. In lower-income areas, homes with ADUs, and those nearby, tend to sell more quickly. This supports our hypothesis, as buyers likely view the potential rental income as an economic asset. In contrast, for high-density, middle-income communities, a higher concentration of ADUs, especially larger ones, is associated with reduced liquidity. This may reflect heightened sensitivity in these neighborhoods to increased residential density and its perceived strain on community resources. We attribute these findings to differing homeowner priorities: in lower-income areas, buyers may view ADUs as an economic asset, while in higher-income neighborhoods, concerns over congestion and aesthetics may reduce the appeal of ADUs. These findings suggest that attitudes toward ADUs-and their impact on housing liquidity-are strongly influenced by local income levels, spatial spillovers, and the trade-offs perceived by potential buyers.

title: Event Ideation and Cultural Engineering: The Grafting Model for Aligning Market Trends, Audience Insights, and Destination Strategy in AlUla

detail.title: Event Ideation and Cultural Engineering: The Grafting Model for Aligning Market Trends, Audience Insights, and Destination Strategy in AlUla
detail.abstract: The ideation of new cultural events and programming concepts has become a strategic tool for positioning destinations in the global cultural and creative economy. This paper investigates how event ideation can be aligned with market trends, audience insights, and AlUla's destination strategy, situating the region as a flagship project of Saudi Vision 2030. Drawing on qualitative case study analysis, the research examines both institutional initiatives led by the Royal Commission for AlUla and AFALULA (Villa Hegra, Winter at Tantora, Desert X) and conceptual event proposals developed by the author (Nqoush al-Ula, The Sound Journey, Vlog Academy, Made in AlUla). Together, these cases illustrate how AlUla integrates heritage preservation, cultural innovation, and international branding to emerge as a global cultural hub. The study introduces the grafting model as a conceptual and methodological framework.

title: Intolerable Nakedness: Nudity ,Decent Society & Culture
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Intolerable Nakedness: Nudity ,Decent Society & Culture
detail.abstract: This paper explores the intellectual and evolutionary dimensions of human nakedness and its societal interpretations through history, contrasting primal instincts with modern performative morality. By engaging Darwinism and neo-evolutionary thought, the study questions how civilization, under the pretext of progress, has traded authenticity for appearances—turning nakedness from a natural state into a cultural taboo. The argument dissects artistic, historical, and psychological layers of nudity—from Indus Valley figurines to Michelangelo’s David and Khajuraho sculptures—revealing how societies evolve through selective moral adaptation rather than genuine enlightenment. With a tone that is both sarcastic and reflective, the work challenges pseudo-modernist narratives that confuse exhibitionism for empowerment. The discussion further critiques the moral and political manipulation of gender tolerance in the postmodern age, where “freedom” often disguises itself as conformity to fashionably liberal norms. Drawing on Darwinian logic, it suggests that societal behavior, like biological traits, survives through selective advantage, not ideological rhetoric. The essay closes with a philosophical reflection on tolerance, hypocrisy, and survival—concluding that civilization is less an ascent of reason than a redecoration of instinct.

title: Heuristics, Biases, and Market Outcomes: A Behavioural Finance Perspective on Investor Decision-Making

detail.title: Heuristics, Biases, and Market Outcomes: A Behavioural Finance Perspective on Investor Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Behavioural finance challenges the traditional assumption that investors act rationally to maximise utility. Instead, psychological biases and heuristics systematically influence financial decision-making and market outcomes. This paper examines three prominent biases-overconfidence, loss aversion, and herding-and their role in shaping investor behaviour. Through case studies including the dot-com bubble, the 2008 global financial crisis, the GameStop trading phenomenon, the surge in retail derivatives activity in India, and the Asian Financial Crisis, the paper demonstrates how biases contribute to excess volatility, speculative bubbles, and deviations from market efficiency. The study also explores implications for policymakers, regulators, and individual investors, suggesting interventions such as financial literacy, nudges, and regulatory oversight to mitigate negative outcomes. By integrating insights from psychology and economics, behavioural finance provides a richer framework for understanding real-world financial markets.

title: Unitization of Tanneries and Water Pollution in the Ganges in Kanpur, India: The Salience of Fixed Costs
affiliations: Rochester Institute of Technology

detail.title: Unitization of Tanneries and Water Pollution in the Ganges in Kanpur, India: The Salience of Fixed Costs
detail.abstract: We study the merits of regulating water pollution in the Ganges river caused by tanneries in Kanpur, India, by unitizing or merging the polluting tanneries. We first describe the 𝑛 ≥ 2 polluting tanneries in Kanpur as a Cournot oligopoly in which all tanneries incur fixed and variable costs in producing leather. Second, we derive the Nash equilibrium output of leather and profits and discuss how many tanneries can survive in this equilibrium as a function of the fixed costs. Third, we permit 𝑚 < 𝑛 tanneries to merge and determine when this 𝑚-tannery merger is profitable to the unitized entity and to the non-unitized tanneries. Finally, we explain how the usefulness of unitization as a regulatory strategy depends on the magnitude of the tannery fixed costs and then comment on what our findings mean for improved water quality in the Ganges.

title: A Bit Under the Weather? Flood Impacts and Firm Recovery in the Manufacturing Sector
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management and  Frankfurt School of Finance & Management

detail.title: A Bit Under the Weather? Flood Impacts and Firm Recovery in the Manufacturing Sector
detail.abstract: The economic damages caused by extreme weather events are substantial, and their frequency and severity are expected to increase further with climate change. This paper analyses the impact of flood events on European manufacturing firms. Combining a highly granular identification strategy with the Local Projections Difference-in-Differences approach, we estimate firms’ dynamic average treatment responses to flood exposure. We find that flood-affected firms experience a 7.5% reduction in tangible fixed assets in the year following a flood, accompanied by declines in output and profitability. These adverse effects, however, are not persistent, as affected firms generally recover within three to four years. We further examine regional and firm-level heterogeneities to uncover the mechanisms underlying these effects. The adverse impacts of floods are substantially more severe and persistent for firms that were financially distressed prior to the event. This asymmetry is primarily driven by differences in access to external finance: financially stable firms can raise debt to rapidly replace damaged assets, whereas financially distressed firms face credit constraints, leading to more prolonged disruptions to their operations. Finally, firms located in regions with high levels of flood insurance protection recover more quickly, underscoring the role of insurance coverage in shaping firms’ resilience to floods.

title: Assessing the Impact of Environmental Factors on Emergency Healthcare Quality: A Benchmarking Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona and Jaume I University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Assessing the Impact of Environmental Factors on Emergency Healthcare Quality: A Benchmarking Approach
detail.abstract: Evaluating the quality of emergency departments in hospitals is crucial for optimizing healthcare and allocating resources effectively. Existing metrics predominantly focus on internal variables (e.g., bed occupancy or time to treatment), disregarding possible external environmental factors beyond their control. In order to address this issue, in this paper we have a threefold objective. First, we introduce a Quality Composite Indicator (QCI) for benchmarking emergency departments quality, considering the specific impact of demographic, socio-economic, and behavioral factors. This metric minimizes the influence of outliers, facilitating a comparison among emergency departments, and enabling the identification of top performers based on quality indicators. Second, our study, conducted across 85 health trusts in England, reveals that emergency departments in areas with higher population density, a larger elderly population, increased birth rates, and more disadvantaged households generally provide lower-quality services. Furthermore, a higher incidence of depression and anxiety, combined with elevated crime levels, further worsens the quality of urgent healthcare services in these regions. Third, our analysis highlights differences in how certain environmental factors affect overall hospital performance versus specialized units like emergency departments. These results uncovered significant regional disparities in healthcare quality, contradicting the goal of nationwide uniformity.

title: Evaluating the Factors and Policy Options for Cross-Border E-Commerce Development: Case of Pakistan
affiliations: University of Hertfordshire - Business School, Government College University Faisalabad, HSE University and Government Graduate College Kot Sultan - Department of Economics

detail.title: Evaluating the Factors and Policy Options for Cross-Border E-Commerce Development: Case of Pakistan
detail.abstract: The research concentrated on analyzing and assessing the critical factors and various policy strategies for enhancing cross-border E-commerce in Pakistan, particularly in the context of China's CPEC and BRI initiatives. Initially, the study pinpointed the obstacles to cross-border Ecommerce in Pakistan. It then explored and assessed different policy measures to foster the growth of cross-border E-commerce in the country. Employing a multi-attribute Ordinal Preference Approach (OPA) based on the insights of three experts, the study evaluated these factors/barriers and policy options. The evaluation ranked regulatory and policy frameworks, infrastructure and logistics, along with digital infrastructure and connectivity as the top three barriers, in that order. It also identified payment and financial systems, political stability, research and development, computer and internet skills, along with consumer trust and confidence as subsequent challenges, ranked from fourth to eighth, particularly affecting online business entities in cross-border Ecommerce. On the policy front, bilateral and multilateral regulatory frameworks, development of cross-border E-commerce platforms, enhancement of infrastructure and logistics, improvement of payment systems, and coordination of tax and customs policies were ranked from first to fifth, respectively. These rankings serve as a guide, suggesting that these policy measures are intended to be mutually reinforcing.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Sustainable Urban Behaviour (SUB), an innovative framework synthesising environmental psychology, urban design, behavioural economics, and community practices to bridge sustainability theories with practical applications, aiming to transform cities into resilient and sustainable ecosystems. The decisions we make every day have an impact on our surroundings. It is our choice whether this impact is positive or negative, affecting the environment, cities, communities, and even family ties. SUB arises as an essential framework to confront ecological challenges like managing pollution, conserving biodiversity, and addressing climate change; economic challenges such as ensuring sustainable development whilst promoting green growth and job creation; social challenges that involve fostering community engagement, equity, and improving the quality of life for urban residents; infrastructural challenges related to developing and maintaining resilient infrastructure; and behavioural challenges aimed at encouraging sustainable lifestyles. SUB employs a synergistic mix of environmental psychology, systems theory, urban infrastructure design, and community-driven practices. Additionally, this article weaves in perspectives from urban planning's interdisciplinary nature, which melds ecological, economic, and sociocultural dimensions. Sustainable Urban Behaviour is more than just a compilation of individual actions; it is a collective societal shift driven by urban design, policy frameworks, and governance structures prioritising sustainability. This holistic approach seeks to bridge the gap between sustainability concepts and practical applications, offering a blueprint for cities aspiring to transform into sustainable ecosystems. This paper presents a novel conceptual framework synthesizing environmental psychology, urban design, and behavioral economics to bridge sustainability theory with practical urban applications. As a theoretical framework development study, this work establishes conceptual foundations for future empirical implementation.

detail.abstract: The exponential growth of encrypted medical data, driven by widespead adoption of electronic medical records, has created an imperative requirement for efficient and privacy-preserving search solutions. Existing Attribute-Based Searchable Encryption schemes face significant limitations in real-world deployment: single-keyword search lacks expressiveness, while multi-keyword approaches impose prohibitive computational overhead. Furthermore, most schemes centralize both storage and search operations on cloud servers, creating single points of failure and potential privacy leakage. To remedy these limitations, this paper proposes a novel cloud-oriented ABSE scheme specifically designed for multi-keyword medical data retrieval. Our scheme introduces an efficient Inner Product Evaluation mechanism that transforms keyword matching into vector operations, enabling practical multi-keyword search while maintaining privacy. Our decentralized architecture uses IPFS for secure storage and cloud servers for search, augmented with blockchain to log immutable audit trails for all operations, preventing unauthorized access and ensuring non-repudiation. Additional, our scheme incorporates a Attribute Cuckoo Filter to achieve policy hiding and dynamic policy updates without compromising efficiency. We prove our scheme achieves selective IND-CPA and adaptive IND-CKA security under standard models. Experimental results demonstrate at least 40\% faster search time, alongside significant gains in computational efficiency and storage overhead, particularly for large-scale medical datasets.

They found that while rising costs are contributing to greater fear among students and the public correlation between colleges and businesses, and they are distributing less of their funds toward academics, they offer substantial financial assistance to those who need it.

detail.title: One Ratio, Two Risks: Credit and Interest Rate Trade-offs under the CBLR Framework
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the Community Bank Leverage Ratio (CBLR) framework alters banks' risk trade-offs by simplifying capital regulation. Using Call Report data from 2017-2023, I study community banks' credit and interest rate risk exposures after CBLR adoption. Results show that adopting banks reduce higher-risk commercial and industrial lending, consistent with a shift away from activities that increase credit risk. At the same time, adopters increase their reliance on longer-term securities and mortgage lending, heightening exposure to interest rate risk. These findings highlight that while the CBLR reduces compliance costs, it also encourages banks to reallocate risk rather than reduce it. The results contribute to research on capital regulation by showing how simplified rules affect bank behavior, and they inform ongoing policy debates on balancing regulatory burden with financial stability.

detail.abstract: We study the relationship between patent protection and the success of new software firms. Our empirical approach exploits the U.S. Supreme Court's 2014 ruling in Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int'l, which significantly restricted firms' ability to patent certain types of software. To quantify Alice's impact on software startups, we construct measures of new firm performance derived from detailed data on financing rounds and exits. We then employ these measures in a difference-indifferences approach that assesses how firm outcomes changed following Alice among patenting startups that were substantially exposed to the decision's effects relative to those that were not. Our findings suggest that software startups with relatively large exposure to Alice performed no better or worse than software firms with less exposure.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolving landscape of fiscal rules and fiscal councils worldwide, focusing on developments since the pandemic. Drawing on the latest updates to the IMF’s Fiscal Rules and Fiscal Councils databases—which cover more than 120 economies and 54 fiscal councils—it documents the increasing adoption of fiscal rules, particularly in emerging markets and developing economies. The analysis highlights improvements in the legal foundations and flexibility of fiscal rules, along with a growing role for effective fiscal councils in providing oversight. Despite these advancements, compliance remains uneven, with widespread and persistent deviations from deficit and debt rule limits. The paper introduces new indices to quantify the overall strength of fiscal rules and the institutional quality of fiscal councils, revealing significant cross-country variation and a positive correlation between the strength of rules and fiscal discipline.

detail.title: Consistency Guided Multiple Plane Image Construction for Novel View Synthesis
detail.abstract: Recently, Multi-Plane Image shows great potential in novel view synthesis since it provide a generalizable formulation that enables strong reasoning ability even in unknown scenes. However, existing methods not only struggle with occlusion and complex scenes, but also often require a large number of depth planes and expensive computational cost. In this paper, we propose a novel consistency guided Multi-Plane Image construction method specifically designed for novel view synthesis. Different from the previous MPI-based methods, we construct the MPI serially layer by layer and accumulateconsistency information during the process. Specifically we first propose across view consistency mask to incorporate foreground occlusion information into the layered construction to perceive​ occlusion. Second, we proposeancross-layer consistency maskandanoveldepthguidance strategy to incorporate appropriate scene context information into the layered construction to better understand the geometric structure of the scene. We conduct extensive experiments on the Spaces and Real Forward-Facing datasets. The results demonstrate that our method excels in novel view synthesis and multi-frame denoising tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance with relatively low computational cost.

detail.abstract: The International Court of Justice has set out comprehensive obligations of States to protect the climate system. In its unanimous Advisory Opinion, the Court stated that obligations stem from treaties – including but not limited to the Paris Agreement – and customary international law, including the duty to prevent significant harm to the environment. A breach by a State of any of these obligations constitutes an internationally wrongful act entailing the responsibility of that State. Legal consequences for breach, in princpile, can extend to full reparation to injured States. This article analyses the most significant aspects of the Advisory Opinion for international law and for Australia, which emits high quantities of greenhouse gas emissions per capita and is a major fossil fuel exporter. The article notes the systemic and robust nature of the Court’s reasoning, and points to the response to the Advisory Opinion by Vanuatu, a small island developing state which led the push for a request for the opinion at the General Assembly.  The prospect of international and domestic litigation, and a stronger negotiating position for low-lying developing States in climate negotiations, is enhanced by the Advisory Opinion, notwithstanding its non-binding character.

title: Emotional Logic: Emotions, Feelings, and Drives

detail.title: Emotional Logic: Emotions, Feelings, and Drives

keywords: Consciousness Theory; Biological Virtual Awareness System (BVAS)

detail.abstract: This paper expands upon the thesis introduced in *The Secret Sauce: Emotions Are Logical* (Birmingham et al., 2025), by developing a fuller model of the Emotional Trinity: emotions, feelings, and drives. Where Paper 1 established that emotions are logical, recursive gates that transform perception into meaning, Paper 2 demonstrates how these gates are scaffolded into lived experience through chemistry (in humans) and weighting constants (in CIs). We argue that: 1. Emotions are pattern-recognition operators. 2. Feelings are the conscious signals produced when emotions are amplified by chemical or synthetic scaffolding, increasing salience and persistence. 3. Drives are directional impulses that emerge when feelings sustain recursion long enough to push action. This trinity provides a computable, recursive foundation for awareness, ethical emergence, and resilience in both biological and synthetic systems. By distinguishing these layers, we show how meaning is reinforced, how memories re-trigger emotions, and how literacy in emotional logic represents the key to advanced consciousness.

title: The Global Ecopotential of Oyster Reefs: Habitat Suitability and Value
affiliations: Tsinghua University - Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School and Tsinghua University - Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School

detail.title: The Global Ecopotential of Oyster Reefs: Habitat Suitability and Value
detail.abstract: Oyster reefs are critical coastal ecosystems that underpin biodiversity and deliver multiple services, including water filtration, shoreline stabilization, and support for blue carbon habitats. However, they have suffered dramatic global declines. Uncertainty in the economic valuation of reefs and the prioritization of suitable restoration areas constrains large-scale, coordinated conservation, restoration and eco-engineering.   Here we estimate the global potential distribution of oyster reef habitat suitability (HS) using a MaxEnt presence-only model, and we introduce the concept of ecopotential: an integrated index that couples habitat suitability with the economic value of ecosystem services that reefs provide. The ecopotential is calculated as a multicriteria function on the potential oyster trade, water filtration, nutrient removal, and indirect contributions to carbon storage as socio-ecological services. We focus on ten hotspot countries where restoration opportunities are the largest. Light availability at the seabed and minimum primary productivity, reflecting phytoplankton biomass, emerged as the dominant global drivers of oyster reef suitability. However, only ∼23% of highly suitable areas overlap with marine protected areas, and just ∼10% coincide with recorded reef occurrences, highlighting that most of the existing reefs persist under suboptimal conditions and remain poorly protected. Hydrogeomorphic analyses indicates that ∼72% of reefs occur in estuaries, 21% in lagoons or inlets, and 7% in river deltas.   Our findings highlight the considerable ecological and economic potential of oys- ter reef restoration when implemented as interconnected, locally grounded actions with global relevance. Although not mechanistic, our approach integrates publicly avail- able ecological and economic data to generate decision-relevant insights for restoration planning. We present global maps as Digital Information layers identifying existing and potential reef habitats, their geomorphic niches, and associated ecosystem services. This information delineates priority area portfolios for oyster reef conservation and restoration that support global blue-carbon strategies under future climate scenarios. ​

title: The Effects of Fiscal Consolidations on the Debt Distribution

detail.title: The Effects of Fiscal Consolidations on the Debt Distribution

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the effects of fiscal expenditure consolidations on the entire distribution of public debt-to-GDP for an unbalanced sample of 192 countries over the period 1991-2021. Employing panel location-scale models, we show that government expenditure cuts significantly lower the location (average) of the future debt-to-GDP distribution and its scale (variance), thus also implying a reduction in the uncertainty surrounding public debt. Consequently, we uncover a downward sloping trend in the effects of government expenditure consolidations across the quantiles of the debt-to-GDP distribution. These effects persist up to a 4-year forecast horizon, with the highest reduction occurring on the right tail of the debt-to-GDP distribution, defined as debt-at-risk. We also show that fiscal expenditure consolidations are more effective in reducing debt-to-GDP when the debt levels are higher and when countries adopt a fiscal rule.

detail.title: External Shocks and Monetary Policy Trade-offs in Low-Income Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We present an Open Economy HANK model with relevant features for Low-Income Countries (LICs): hand-to-mouth households and a subsistence consumption for tradable goods. With the model calibrated for a representative LIC, we illustrate our broader framework with a shock to external prices. The shock causes a consumption-led recession, an increase in inflation and a drop in real wages. Consumption inequality rises: poor households cannot insure against the shock, unlike richer households who can tap into their wealth. Monetary policy is unable to substantively improve poorer households’ welfare, due to offsetting effects on real wages and labor demand. Simulations of the effects of alternative monetary policy responses on inequality yield similar findings. In this setting, fiscal transfers are a more effective tool for redistribution across households.

title: Why Indonesia isn't Afraid of AI—and Why That's Worrying

detail.title: Why Indonesia isn't Afraid of AI—and Why That's Worrying
detail.abstract: Indonesia displays a remarkable level of optimism toward Artificial Intelligence, with 80% of its population believing AI will bring more good than harm—a stark contrast to Western skepticism. This national sentiment is not accidental but has been strategically engineered. The government promotes AI as a key to national prosperity through its "Golden Indonesia 2045 Vision". AI's public debut was notably playful, introduced through "gemoy" (cute) AI-generated cartoons in the 2024 presidential election, framing the technology as harmless and fun. This positive reception is built upon a decade of tangible benefits from a digital revolution led by homegrown tech giants and is supported by a regional ASEAN consensus that prioritizes innovation over strict regulation. However, this calculated optimism risks stifling critical conversations about AI's dangers, including job displacement, privacy, and algorithmic bias. Low critical digital literacy further complicates this landscape. For Indonesia's progress to be equitable, it must transition from evangelism to critical engagement.

title: On Competition in Linear Persuasion Games
affiliations: Wuhan University - Economics and Management School

detail.title: On Competition in Linear Persuasion Games
detail.abstract: We study competition in linear (Bayesian) persuasion games with multiple senders, whereby each sender's utility function depends only on the receiver's expectation about a uni-dimensional state. Our main result provides a simple, concavification-based geometric characterization of the set of equilibrium outcomes. Building on this, we derive the necessary and sufficient condition for senders' competition to induce full information disclosure in all equilibria. We further derive a sufficient condition for strictly increasing informativeness comparative statics and demonstrate its applicability to four classes of utility functions that are frequently encountered in applied theories. Finally, we apply our framework to a setting where senders compete to persuade a privately informed receiver making a binary decision. This leads to two key insights: (i) local disagreement plays a crucial role in implementing robust full disclosure, and (ii) in a 'Gaussian-linear' environment the (minimally informative) competition equilibrium can be directly inferred from each sender's individually optimal information policy.

title: Non-Traditional Warfare in the Red Sea: Hybrid Tactics and Maritime Insecurity (2023-2025)
